![The import is part of the analysis: the observations on these sheets need to retain their meaning when they reach R. Illustration generated with ChatGPT.](/assets/images/projects/tidycreel-connect.png){fig-alt="Watercolor illustration inside a lakeside fisheries field office. Separate stacks of survey sheets sit beside a laptop displaying several tables, while a person holds another sheet for review."}

The examples in this series have usually begin with tables that are already in
R. Real creel data often have another step before that. Interviews might arrive
in a CSV export, counts might live in a database, and fish measurements might
come from a separate table. Complicating things further, each source has its own
names and codes.

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chrischizinski/tidycreel.connect/main/man/figures/logo.png){fig-alt="Tidycreel.connect logo" width=180px fig-align="center"}

That is the part of the workflow handled by **tidycreel.connect**, which now has
its own [repository](https://github.com/chrischizinski/tidycreel.connect). It
provides a foundation that reads source tables and maps them to the names and
values that tidycreel expects. The survey design and estimation can then follow
from there.

The practical question is simple: **Can we describe an export once and reuse
that description every time we load it?** In this post, we'll use a small CSV
example to explore what that description should include and what still requires
our attention each time new data arrive.

## Describing the Data Source and Survey Design

The [linked-tables post](/posts/2026-09-18-linked-tables.html) asked what one
row represents. That distinction remains important when importing data. A single
trip may include catches of multiple species but still represents one interview,
while multiple counts conducted on the same date represent separate
observations.

A *connection profile* describes the source: where its tables are, which columns
contain the needed information, and what its codes mean. The *survey design*
describes how observations were sampled: the calendar, strata, selection
probabilities, and field protocol. We need both.

![The profile describes the source. The sampling plan supplies the information needed to interpret the observations. Loading tables does not establish their sampling design.](/assets/images/projects/tidycreel-connect-workflow.svg){#fig-connect-workflow fig-alt="A source and a connection profile feed tidycreel.connect. Counts, interviews, catch, and lengths remain separate tables. Those tables and a separate sampling plan feed tidycreel for design declaration and estimation."}

For example, a profile can tell us that `HoursFished` is the source's effort
column. We still need to know whether those hours describe one angler or a
party. Renaming the column cannot answer that question.

## Start with a small export we can inspect

The [complete R
script](/assets/code/tidycreel_connect_walkthrough.R){download="tidycreel_connect_walkthrough.R"}
creates five fictional CSV files and a connection profile, loads the files,
checks the results, and attaches the tables to a design. Download it and run it
in an R session. It creates a new temporary directory each time and prints its
location; the files remain available during that session. No database account is
needed.

### Install from GitHub

**tidycreel.connect is currently available only on GitHub.** I have no plans to
submit it to CRAN at this time. This example also uses the development version
of tidycreel. Install both packages from GitHub with `pak`:

```r
# Install pak once, if needed.
install.packages("pak")

# Install both GitHub packages and config for this example.
pak::pak(c(
  "chrischizinski/tidycreel",
  "chrischizinski/tidycreel.connect",
  "config"
))
```

Then run the downloaded example:

```r
# Run after saving the download in your working directory.
source("tidycreel_connect_walkthrough.R")
```

The `config` package is needed for the YAML profile used here. The walkthrough
was checked with tidycreel **8.0.0.9000** at commit
[`cd02a018`](https://github.com/chrischizinski/tidycreel/tree/cd02a018c044d5aec5ccba605513bd191a7dbed0)
and tidycreel.connect **0.5.0** at
[`b592b8a`](https://github.com/chrischizinski/tidycreel.connect/tree/b592b8a121daf1a9ae9c8f749c132afad7de180f).
These are GitHub builds; the script includes installation commands for those
exact revisions. The code below walks through the objects created by the script.

Our fictional fishery permits shore fishing only. The survey has eight
completed-trip interviews and two instantaneous counts on each of four sampled
dates. All parties were interviewed at the access point after fishing, and
everyone in a party fished for the reported trip duration.

The first three interviews arrive like this:

  | TripID  | HoursFished | PartySize | TotalFish | TripCode |
  | :------ | ----------: | --------: | --------: | :------- |
  | trip-01 |           2 |         2 |         3 | C        |
  | trip-02 |           3 |         1 |         0 | C        |
  | trip-03 |           1 |         1 |         2 | C        |

For `trip-01`, two anglers fished for two hours each and caught three fish
between them. For `trip-02`, one angler fished for three hours and caught
nothing. Both interviews belong in the analysis.

## Map the names and explain the codes

The script writes a YAML file, `creel-config.yml`. YAML is a text format that
allows us to define the data source separately from the analysis code. The files
section specifies the paths to the five CSV files, while the `schema` section
identifies the relevant columns and codes. Although the script generates this
file, it can also be created or edited outside of R using any text editor. This
makes it possible to share a common configuration among users working with the
same data sources, without requiring each person to define the connections
independently.

Here is the interview portion of that profile; the download contains the
complete profile for all five files:

```yaml
schema:
  survey_type: instantaneous
  columns:
    interview_uid: TripID
    date: SurveyDate
    effort: HoursFished
    n_anglers: PartySize
    catch: TotalFish
    trip_status: TripCode
  strata_cols:
    day_type: DayType
  value_maps:
    trip_status:
      "C": complete
```

Read each column entry as **the name the package expects: the name in our
export**. The `value_maps` entry does a different job: it says that our source
uses `C` for a completed trip. That meaning comes from the source documentation.
The package cannot infer it from the letter.

The distinction between `catch` and `catch_count` is important. In this profile,
`catch` maps to `TotalFish`, the total catch reported for an interview. The
fetched interview table names this column `catch_count`. In contrast, the
profile's `catch_count` entry maps to `FishCount`, the number of fish recorded
for each species in the separate catch-detail file. The complete example
includes both mappings.

After loading, the same first three interviews look like this:

  | interview_uid | effort | n_anglers | catch_count | trip_status |
  | :------------ | -----: | --------: | ----------: | :---------- |
  | trip-01       |      2 |         2 |           3 | complete    |
  | trip-02       |      3 |         1 |           0 | complete    |
  | trip-03       |      1 |         1 |           2 | complete    |

The observations have not changed. The names and trip-status code now have an
explicit translation. Dates are read as dates and numeric fields are coerced and
checked. Party size remains available for the later calculation of angler-hours.

## Fetch each table without flattening the survey

With the profile written, loading the data takes a connection and the
appropriate fetch functions:

```r
library(tidycreel)
library(tidycreel.connect)

conn <- creel_connect_from_yaml(profile_path)

interviews <- fetch_interviews(conn)
counts <- fetch_counts(conn)
catch_data <- fetch_catch(conn)
harvest_lengths <- fetch_harvest_lengths(conn)
release_lengths <- fetch_release_lengths(conn)
```

Here, `profile_path` points to the YAML file created by our script. When working
with your own data, replace it with the path to your own yaml file.

The tables remain separate. In this example, the row counts before and after
fetching are:

  | Table | Source rows | Fetched rows | What one row represents |
  | :------ | ------------: | -------------: | :------------------------ |
  | Interviews | 8 | 8 | A completed trip by an angler or party |
  | Counts | 8 | 8 | An instantaneous count at a recorded time |
  | Catch | 7 | 7 | A species and catch type within an interview |
  | Harvest lengths | 2 | 2 | A measured harvested fish |
  | Release lengths | 0 | 0 | No measurements collected |

The catch file has seven rows because one interview has two species and two
interviews have zero catch. That arrangement is intentional. Joining the catch
file onto the interviews and summing repeated trip hours would change what the
total represents.

The CSV connection currently requires paths for all five tables. When no release
lengths were collected, the example supplies an empty CSV with the appropriate
headers. An empty measurements table does not establish how many fish were
released; that information belongs in the catch records.

## Validate the Imported Data

I want to check a few things while the export and the imported tables are still
easy to compare. The script verifies that interview identifiers and count times
survived, catch and length records link to known interviews, and the interview
totals agree with the catch-detail totals in this example.

```r

checks <- c(
  interview_ids_preserved = identical(
    interviews$interview_uid, raw_interviews$TripID
  ),
  count_times_preserved = identical(
    counts$count_time, raw_counts$CountClock
  ),
  catch_records_linked = all(
    catch_data$interview_uid %in% interviews$interview_uid
  ),
  zero_catch_interviews = sum(interviews$catch_count == 0) == 2L
)

print(checks)
```

The last check is specific to data we constructed. A real export needs checks
based on what its records mean. In particular, an absent catch-detail row cannot
establish whether the interview had zero catch or whether its catch information
is missing.

  | Source meaning               | Value after import   | What it tells us                     |
  | :---------------             | :------------------- | :-----------------                   |
  | The party caught no fish     | `0`                  | Observed zero catch                  |
  | Catch was not recorded       | `NA`                 | Catch is unknown                     |
  | No matching catch-detail row | No row               | Consult the source's recording rules |

The download also makes a separate demonstration copy with one unknown catch
value and verifies that it remains `NA` after fetching. That copy is kept out of
the design. We should resolve unknown values according to the survey records
before estimation, without substituting zeros to make a check pass.

Also read messages about columns that were not carried through. An unused
administrative field may be harmless; a missing stratum, party size, or count
time can change the analysis. The [diagnostics
post](/posts/2026-10-09-reading-diagnostics.html) picks up those checks after
the tables are attached.

## Bring the sampling plan back in

The source files contain observations from four dates. Our fictional survey
season contains nine dates. The calendar needs all nine, including days on which
no sampling occurred, as discussed in the [sampling-calendar
post](/posts/2026-09-03-sampling-calendar.html).

The example assumes equal day-selection probabilities within weekday and weekend
strata. Each sampled day covers the entire eight-hour fishing period; there is
no random selection of one shift from several. We therefore supply eight actual
hours and a period-selection probability of one.

```r
counts$period_hours <- 8

design <- creel_design(calendar, date = date, strata = day_type) |>
  add_counts(
    counts,
    count_col = bank_anglers,
    count_time_col = count_time,
    period_length_col = period_hours,
    p_period = 1
  ) |>
  add_interviews(
    interviews,
    catch = catch_count,
    effort = effort,
    trip_status = trip_status,
    trip_duration = effort,
    n_anglers = n_anglers,
    interview_type = "access"
  ) |>
  add_catch(
    catch_data,
    catch_uid = interview_uid,
    interview_uid = interview_uid,
    species = species,
    count = catch_count,
    catch_type = catch_type
  )
```

Using `bank_anglers` as the count is appropriate here because the fictional
fishery has only shore fishing. A survey that also counts fishing boats needs
the boat component represented and converted appropriately. Likewise, the
eight-hour period and probability of one describe this example's protocol; they
are not general defaults for a creel survey.

The `count_time_col` argument tells tidycreel that the two counts on each date
are repeated observations within a sampled day. The resulting design reports
four daily count observations, while retaining the information for within-day
variation. The fetch step returned all eight source counts.

For `add_catch()`, both linking arguments select the interview identifier in
their respective tables. Despite its name, the `catch_uid` argument here does
**not** select the unique catch-row identifier. The script also attaches the
measured fish through their interview links.

We now have a design containing the imported observations and the declared
sampling information. The [design-object
post](/posts/2026-08-27-design-object.html) explains why keeping those together
matters. This example stops at that handoff so we can inspect it before asking
for estimates.

## A separate repository for the connection work

`tidycreel.connect` now lives in its own repository, with separate
[documentation](https://chrischizinski.com/tidycreel.connect/) and [issue
tracker](https://github.com/chrischizinski/tidycreel.connect/issues). The
separation reflects the different responsibilities of the two packages.
`tidycreel.connect` handles the differences among data sources, translating them
into a consistent set of tables, while `tidycreel` uses those tables to define
survey designs and calculate estimates. Keeping these functions separate allows
data connections to change without affecting the analytical methods and lets
users work directly with `tidycreel` when their data are already in the expected
format.

## Connecting Different Data Sources

The CSV example illustrates in this post is only one way to bring data into the
tidycreel workflow. `tidycreel.connect` also supports databases through DBI,
including SQL Server via ODBC, and REST APIs configured through a profile. For
CSV files and databases, the `schema` defines how source columns map to the
expected fields. API profiles instead specify mappings for endpoint fields. Each
data source requires its own description, but the resulting tables follow a
common structure that can be used throughout the analysis.

Once a connection profile has been established, it can be reused for subsequent
exports that follow the same data structure and recording conventions. This
reduces the need to repeatedly define column mappings and interpret
source-specific codes. However, changes to the data structure or field protocols
may require updates to the profile, the survey design, or both.

In the next post, we'll bring these connection profiles, validation checks, and
survey design decisions into a Quarto report alongside the resulting estimates.
This will provide a documented path from the original data to the final results.
